title: How do hotels make money, and what matters in a hotel case?
description: Hotel economics for case interviews: occupancy, average daily rate, RevPAR, fixed costs, franchising and online travel agents, with a worked RevPAR example.
hook: Hotels make money by selling a perishable product, tonight's room, at the best mix of price and occupancy, on top of mostly fixed property and staff costs, with extra income from food, drink and meeting space. Since an empty room tonight can never be sold again, almost every hotel case comes down to occupancy, average room rate, the cost of each booking channel and who owns versus who brands the hotel.
body:
The measures that matter

MeasureFormula
OccupancyRooms sold ÷ rooms available
Average daily rate (ADR)Room revenue ÷ rooms sold
RevPAR (revenue per available room)Occupancy × ADR, or room revenue ÷ rooms available
Profit per available roomOccupancy × (ADR − variable cost per occupied room)

RevPAR is the industry's favourite measure because it combines price and occupancy in one number. Its weakness is that it ignores cost: every occupied room needs cleaning, laundry and amenities, and some bookings carry a commission. That is why the last row matters.

A worked example: price versus occupancy

Two illustrative hotels:

  • Hotel A: 80% occupancy at $150. RevPAR = $120.
  • Hotel B: 70% occupancy at $180. RevPAR = $126.

Hotel B earns more per room despite being emptier. Add a variable cost of $35 per occupied room and the gap widens: A earns 80% × ($150 − $35) = $92 per available room, B earns 70% × ($180 − $35) = $101.50. Fuller is not automatically better.

Now take a 200-room hotel like A. Over a year, room revenue is 200 × 365 × $120 = $8.76M, before food, drink and meetings. Management raises the rate to $170, but occupancy slips to 65%. RevPAR falls to $110.50, and profit per available room to 65% × ($170 − $35) = $87.75, both worse than before. Price rises and discounts both need testing on the same basis: what happens to profit per available room, not to rate or occupancy alone.

Who owns what

A hotel can involve three separate businesses: the owner of the building, the operator that runs it and the brand on the sign. Many large hotel groups own very few of their hotels. Hilton, for example, owns or leases only a small fraction of the hotels carrying its brands; the rest belong to independent owners who pay franchise or management fees. Fees are often a percentage of room revenue, so a brand charging an illustrative 5% on the hotel above earns $438k a year without investing in the building. That asset-light model lets brands grow quickly with little capital, while owners take the property risk.

Channels and commissions

Online travel agencies (OTAs) such as Booking.com and Expedia bring guests but charge a commission, commonly 15% or more of the booking value. At an 18% commission, a $150 room booked through an OTA brings the hotel $123, against $150 booked directly. That is why hotels push loyalty programmes and direct booking, while still needing OTAs to fill rooms, especially for independent hotels without a big brand.

Typical hotel case questions

  • Why has RevPAR fallen? (occupancy, rate, segment, season)
  • Should we discount in the off-season?
  • Should we overbook to cover guests who don't show up?
  • How can we reduce reliance on online travel agents?
  • Should we buy hotels, or grow by franchising?

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "Occupancy is only 60%, so we should cut prices to fill the hotel."
Strong: "Before discounting, I'd check whether the extra guests would cover the lower rate plus the cost of each occupied room. I'd also split demand into weekday business and weekend leisure, because a discount that works for one could just give money away to the other."

Common mistakes

  • Maximising occupancy. The goal is profit, and a full hotel at a low rate can earn less than a fuller-priced emptier one.
  • Stopping at RevPAR. It ignores the cost of each occupied room and commission by channel.
  • Averaging across segments. Business and leisure guests, weekdays and weekends, peak and off-peak behave differently. Segment first.
  • Confusing owner and brand. A franchise decision looks very different from the owner's side and the brand's side.

Practise

1. A hotel sells rooms at $200 with 60% occupancy. It considers cutting the rate to $160. What occupancy keeps RevPAR the same? With a $40 variable cost per occupied room, what occupancy keeps profit the same?

Show the answer

RevPAR today: 60% × $200 = $120. At $160 it needs $120 ÷ $160 = 75%. Profit per available room today: 60% × ($200 − $40) = $96. At $160 it needs $96 ÷ ($160 − $40) = 80%. The cost test is stricter than the RevPAR test.

2. Out of 1,000 room-nights at $150, 600 come through OTAs at 18% commission. What do commissions cost, and what does moving 100 of those nights to direct booking save?

Show the answer

Commission per OTA night: $150 × 18% = $27. Total: 600 × $27 = $16,200 per 1,000 room-nights. Moving 100 nights saves 100 × $27 = $2,700, less whatever the direct booking push costs.

3. A hotel group can buy a hotel for $40M that would earn it 8% a year, or franchise the same hotel to an owner and earn $500k a year in fees. Which is better?

Show the answer

Owning earns $40M × 8% = $3.2M a year but ties up $40M. Franchising earns $500k with almost no capital, and the $40M could back many more franchised hotels or go back to shareholders. If brand demand is strong enough to sign franchisees, franchising usually gives a far higher return on capital, at the cost of less control over the guest experience.

Where to practise next

Try the Harbourview Hotel case (an off-season discount), the Alder Grand Hotel case (overbooking) and the Heatherfield Hotels case (a laundry investment). For the cost logic, read operating leverage and airline cases, which share the same perishable-capacity economics.
